analysis.one_liner: Requires farm equipment makers to sell repair parts, tools, software, and manuals to owners and independent shops.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee vote or any floor action before the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: Modern tractors and combines are computers on wheels: when one breaks, the manufacturer's digital locks, proprietary software, and parts-pairing requirements often mean only an authorized dealer can fix it. This bill would require manufacturers to make repair documentation, parts, software, and diagnostic tools available to equipment owners and independent repair shops — manuals and software for free, tools at no charge to owners, parts on fair terms and without restrictive registration or pairing requirements. It would be enforced by the Federal Trade Commission. The bill was introduced in September 2023, sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Farmers, ranchers, and farm workers who own or lease equipment, plus independent repair shops and mechanics. Farmers would be able to fix a broken combine during harvest instead of waiting days for a dealer technician, and independent shops could compete for that work.

how_it_helps.text: Manufacturers must make repair documentation, parts, software, firmware, and diagnostic tools available to owners and independent repair providers on fair and reasonable terms [S2].
Documentation must be free (except shipping for a printed copy), and repair tools must be free to equipment owners and cost independent shops no more than authorized dealers pay [S2].
Parts must work without being registered, paired with, or approved by the manufacturer first, and manufacturers cannot force owners to become authorized dealers to use a part or tool [S2].
Owners may legally bypass the electronic locks manufacturers use to block repair, and manufacturers must provide what is needed to disable those locks [S2].
Owners get access to the data their own equipment generates, and violations are enforced by the FTC as unfair or deceptive practices [S2].
The bill preserves trade-secret protections and bars modifications that disable safety systems or break emissions or copyright law, addressing the manufacturers' main stated concerns [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Farm equipment manufacturers and their dealer networks, led by companies like John Deere, would lose part of their highly profitable service-and-parts business, which currently depends on being the only channel able to repair modern machines.
analysis.who_pays_short: Farm equipment makers and dealer service departments

drawbacks.text: Compliance would cost manufacturers real money: they would have to maintain and publish repair documentation, software, and tools for every machine line, revenue their dealer service networks now capture [S2].

Manufacturers argue that opening repair software and security functions to outsiders risks tampering, cybersecurity exposure, and liability when repairs go wrong; the bill's limitations section bars safety and emissions tampering and preserves trade secrets, but critics say enforcement of those lines is easier to promise than to police [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to farmers is concrete and immediate: a machine down during planting or harvest costs real money for every idle day, and dealer-only repair means long waits and dealer pricing. The costs fall on a small set of very large manufacturers, which would keep selling equipment and could still perform dealer service — they would simply have to share what is needed to fix the machines people already bought. The bill carves out the serious objections (trade secrets, safety systems, emissions compliance), making the tradeoff weigh clearly in favor of equipment owners.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in committee: it was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to a subcommittee, and no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever happened before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Marie Gluesenkamp Perez introduced the Agricultural Right to Repair Act on September 20, 2023 [S1].
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce, and two days later to that committee's Subcommittee on Innovation, Data, and Commerce [S4].
Nine Democratic cosponsors signed on; no Republican did [S3].
The subcommittee and full committee took no further action — no markup or vote — and the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, killing the bill [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Farm equipment manufacturers keep their dealer-only repair system, so farmers keep paying dealer service prices and waiting for dealer appointments when machines break down.

sides.party_line_note: All nine cosponsors were Democrats and the sponsor is a Democrat; no Republican signed on, and the Republican-led committee never moved the bill.

industries.industry: Farm equipment manufacturers (John Deere, CNH, AGCO, Kubota)
industries.note: The bill would end the makers' lock on repairing the machines they sell: dealers and manufacturers currently capture service revenue because proprietary software, parts pairing, and digital locks keep owners and independent shops out. Their gain under the status quo is farmers' cost in delays and dealer pricing. (This bill died, so the loss never took effect.)

industries.industry: Independent farm equipment repair shops and mechanics
industries.note: Access to manuals, tools, parts, and repair software would let independent shops compete for repair work they are currently locked out of, and let owners fix machines themselves. (Again, only under the bill — which did not pass.)

Dealer service is the exclusive repair channel today; independent competition would cut into that business. Dealer departments are part of the manufacturers' authorized network the bill defines. (Status quo preserved.)
